h1:
Planning Your Sing Buri Trip
Best Time, Budget & What to Wear
intro: Sing Buri is a low-key province that's incredibly easy to reach — just an hour and a half to two hours' drive from Bangkok. You can do it all in a single day: pay respects at the temples, trace the story of the Bang Rachan war heroes, and eat grilled Mae La snakehead fish by the river. It also pairs easily with Ang Thong or Lopburi in one trip. To keep things smooth, though, you'll want to prep a few things — timing, what to wear inside temples, and what to bring along. We've put it all on one page for you.

blocks.html: Sing Buri suits anyone who wants a short temple-and-history trip without staying overnight. It's about 135 kilometers from Bangkok, roughly a 1.5 to 2 hour drive. From Ang Thong it's even closer — just 20–30 minutes — and from Lopburi it's only about 30–40 minutes, since all three provinces sit right next to each other. That's why a lot of people pair Sing Buri with Ang Thong or Lopburi in one trip. Here's what you should know before you set off.

blocks.text: When Is the Best Time to Visit Sing Buri

blocks.html: The cool season (November–February) is the best window. The weather is comfortable and the sun isn't as harsh as in the hot months, so you can walk around the Bang Rachan war heroes monument and pay respects in open temple courtyards without suffering. Sing Buri sits on the flat central plain along the Chao Phraya and Noi rivers, and many of its temples and memorials are wide open spaces under direct sun. If you go in the hot season (March–May), the afternoon heat can be brutal enough that walking around becomes a chore.

The rainy season (June–October) is fine too — the rice fields along the road turn lush and green, and there are fewer people about, but you'll need to brace for afternoon showers and pack an umbrella. Some temple courtyards can get muddy. The busiest times are long weekends and merit-making festivals like New Year, Songkran, and major Buddhist holy days. If you'd rather not deal with crowds at Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi or the popular snakehead-fish restaurants, skipping public holidays makes for a much easier day.

blocks.title: Timing tip
blocks.html: Leave Bangkok early (before 7am) and you'll reach your first stop mid-morning while the sun is still gentle, with time to see several spots before noon. Most temples in Sing Buri open around 8am to 5pm, and the riverside snakehead-fish restaurants are best reached a little before noon, since they get crowded over the lunch break.

blocks.text: Getting There from Bangkok, Ang Thong or Lopburi

blocks.html: The most convenient option is to drive yourself, because Sing Buri's sights are spread across different districts — the town center, Khai Bang Rachan district, and the riverside — with no public transport linking them. Having your own car gives you the most freedom. From Bangkok, take Highway 32 (the Asia Highway) through Ayutthaya and Ang Thong, then turn off into Sing Buri.

items: Private car — about 1.5–2 hrs from Bangkok, 20–30 min from Ang Thong, 30–40 min from Lopburi. Most flexible, and you can hit several stops in one day.

Van / bus — catch one from Mo Chit 2 (Chatuchak) to Sing Buri. Fares run about ฿130–180 each way and the ride takes around 2–3 hrs, but once you reach town you'll still need to hire a local ride to get to the sights.
Car with driver / chartered taxi — the easiest option for a group; split between you it's good value, and you can cover every stop in a day without worrying about onward transport.
Multi-province pairing — since Sing Buri, Ang Thong and Lopburi sit side by side, many people plan a two-day trip: Sing Buri and Ang Thong on day one, then Lopburi the next.

blocks.title: If you're not driving yourself
blocks.html: We suggest taking a van into Sing Buri town and chartering a local ride for the whole day, or chartering a round-trip car from Ang Thong or Lopburi — because hopping between the sights on your own is fairly awkward. A full-day charter works out better value and you won't be left stranded waiting for a ride back.

blocks.text: How Much Does a Day in Sing Buri Cost

blocks.html: The nice thing about Sing Buri is how affordable it is. Most temples and memorials are free to enter — there's just a donation box for whatever you feel like giving. So your main costs are transport and food, especially that famous Mae La snakehead-fish meal. Here's a rough per-person estimate for a self-drive day trip from Bangkok.

items.name: Fuel + tolls (split)
items.blurb: The Bangkok–Sing Buri round trip is about 270 km. Split between 4 people it comes to just a few hundred baht each; add a bit if you also detour to Ang Thong or Lopburi.

items.name: Two meals + drinks
items.blurb: A riverside grilled Mae La snakehead-fish meal plus another meal of noodles or rice with curry, with a riverside café coffee thrown in. The grilled fish runs a touch pricier than your average meal.

items.name: Donations + offerings
items.blurb: Flowers, incense, candles, gold leaf, and whatever you put in the donation box — no minimum, give as you like.

items.name: Souvenirs
items.blurb: Sun-dried snakehead fish, processed fish products, Thai sweets, or local snacks from the Ban Rachan market to take home as keepsakes.

blocks.html: All in, a Sing Buri day trip runs comfortably around ฿600–1,200 per person if you drive together and split the fuel. It's genuinely good value for a temple-and-history trip, since there's almost nothing to pay at the gate. The one bigger expense is the snakehead-fish meal — and that's well worth it for the flavor.

blocks.text: What to Wear at the Temples

blocks.html: Most Sing Buri trips involve visiting temples and memorials, so dressing modestly matters — both to respect the sites and to get into the sacred areas without being turned away. The simple rule is: cover your shoulders, cover your knees, and avoid anything too tight or see-through.

items: Top — sleeved (short sleeves are fine), covering the shoulders. No spaghetti straps, tube tops or sleeveless cuts. Avoid sheer, see-through fabrics.
Trousers / skirt — long or at least knee-covering. Skip shorts above the knee and short skirts, especially inside the assembly hall at Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi.
Shoes — pick something easy to slip off, since you'll need to remove them before entering ordination and assembly halls. Sandals or easy-on sneakers work best.
Colors / patterns — keep it neat and modest. Avoid loud prints or slogans that might come across as inappropriate.

blocks.title: Carry a cover-up
blocks.html: If you've worn a sleeveless top or shorts that day, tuck a shawl or a small sarong into your bag to drape on when entering the halls — that way you won't waste the trip. Some temples lend out cloths, but not all of them do.

Because many of Sing Buri's sights are open spaces under full sun — both the Bang Rachan war heroes monument and the temple courtyards — and you'll be slipping your shoes on and off a lot, these few things make the day far more comfortable.

items: Hat + sunglasses + sunscreen — the monument grounds and temple courtyards are hot and exposed, with plenty of walking out in the open.
Folding umbrella — doubles as sun and rain cover, and it's a must in the rainy season.
Drinking water — carry a bottle; you'll work up a sweat walking between the stops.
Cash + small notes — for donation boxes, offerings and souvenirs at the markets. Many riverside spots and market stalls still don't take transfers, so bring plenty of ฿20–100 notes.
Socks (if you dislike hot floors) — the hall floors can get hot in the afternoon; socks make walking more comfortable.
Handkerchief / wet wipes — for wiping sweat and cleaning your hands after lighting incense and candles or eating grilled fish.

blocks.text: A Sample Sing Buri Day-Trip Plan

blocks.html: If you're driving from Bangkok and want to cover it all — temples, history, and a standout meal — here's a route that flows without doubling back. Start with the temples in town, then loop out toward Khai Bang Rachan.

items.note: Pay respects to the large reclining Buddha, around 47 meters long, in Sukhothai style — an ancient temple central to Sing Buri's identity. Go early while the sun is still mild.

items.activity: Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Phae temple)
items.note: See the large Buddha image and the Luang Pho Phae hall, dedicated to one of Sing Buri's renowned monks. The grounds are spacious and easy to stroll.
A riverside grilled-fish restaurant along the Asia Highway, such as Mae La Pla Phao or one of the places in Mae La subdistrict. Order salt-grilled snakehead with neem shoots and sweet fish sauce.

items.activity: Bang Rachan war heroes monument + museum
items.note: Trace the story of the Bang Rachan villagers who held off the Burmese army for months. There's a museum on site that tells the history.
Wander the recreated Bang Rachan village market — plenty of food and souvenirs at friendly prices (open only on certain days, so check before you go).
You'll reach Bangkok around evening, in time for dinner at home.

blocks.html: With two days, it's worth tacking on Ang Thong or Lopburi since they're right next door. Spend the first day in Sing Buri on this plan and stay the night, then on day two carry on to Ang Thong to pay respects to the giant Luang Pho Yai Buddha at Wat Muang, or to Lopburi to see Phra Prang Sam Yot and the Phra Narai Ratchaniwet palace. Either way it slots in neatly.

items.note: Pay respects at Wat Phra Non Chakkrasi and Wat Phikun Thong, eat Mae La snakehead fish, trace the Bang Rachan trail, then stay overnight in town.
See Phra Prang Sam Yot, the Phra Narai Ratchaniwet palace, and Lopburi old town before driving back to Bangkok in the evening.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Sing Buri?
faq.a: The cool season, roughly November to February, is the best window — comfortable weather, gentle sun, and you can walk the Bang Rachan monument and pay respects in open temple courtyards without suffering. The hot season turns brutal in the afternoons, while the rainy season brings lush green rice fields but you'll need to plan around afternoon showers.

faq.q: How much does a day in Sing Buri cost?
faq.a: If you drive together and split the fuel, around ฿600–1,200 per person covers it comfortably, since most temples and memorials are free to enter. Your main costs are transport, food and souvenirs. The grilled Mae La snakehead-fish meal runs a touch pricier than an average meal, but it's well worth it for the flavor.

faq.q: What should I wear to the temples in Sing Buri?
faq.a: Dress modestly: cover your shoulders and knees, wear a sleeved top (no spaghetti straps or sleeveless cuts), and choose trousers or a skirt that covers the knees. Pick shoes that slip off easily since you'll remove them before entering the halls, and carry a small shawl in case a temple is strict about dress.

faq.q: Can I combine Sing Buri with Ang Thong or Lopburi?
faq.a: Easily — all three provinces sit side by side. Sing Buri to Ang Thong is just 20–30 minutes, and to Lopburi about 30–40 minutes. Many people plan a two-day trip, doing Sing Buri and Ang Thong one day and Lopburi the next, though you can also just stop at a single province.

faq.q: Can I visit Sing Buri without a car?
faq.a: Yes, but it takes more planning, since the sights are spread across different districts with no public transport linking them. The easiest approach is to take a van or bus from Mo Chit 2 into Sing Buri town and charter a local ride for the day, or charter a round-trip car from Ang Thong or Lopburi.
